t: #2449 Minimum Number of Operations to Make Arrays Similar
o: An operation adds 2 to one element and removes 2 from another, so parity of every element is invariant — odd values must map to odd values. Within each parity class, sorting both arrays and pairing them in order minimizes total movement (an exchange argument shows crossing pairs never help). Each unit of |difference| is 2, and each operation supplies +2 on one side and −2 on another, i.e., 4 units of total |diff|. Hence answer = Σ|paired difference| / 4. Example 1: evens sorted [6,8,12] vs [2,10,14] → diffs 4+2+2=8 → 2 ops. Example 2: odds [1,5] vs [1,3] (diff 2) plus evens [2] vs [4] (diff 2) → 4/4 = 1.
k: Parity is invariant under ±2 operations, so match odds with odds and evens with evens.
Sorted-order pairing minimizes Σ|diff| within each class.
Each operation contributes 4 to Σ|diff|, so the answer is Σ|diff| / 4.

a.n: Approach 1: Parity split + sort + pairwise differences
a.i: Split both arrays by parity, sort each of the four lists, sum absolute pairwise differences, divide by 4.
s: Filter nums and target into odd/even lists; sort all four.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting the four parity lists dominates.

w: One clean approach suffices here. Pitfalls: forgetting the divisibility-by-4 (not 2), assuming parity classes have equal sizes (guaranteed by similarity feasibility), and integer overflow in Java/C++ (use 64-bit accumulation). Follow-up: what if operations were ±1 instead of ±2 (answer becomes Σ|diff|/2 with free parity), or if only k operations were allowed?
